fields.explanation: One join sends a single statement and lets the planner fetch the matching rows together, while the loop pays a round trip per row - the N+1 pattern, whose cost is latency rather than work. Treat it as a trade-off, not a rule: joining a one-to-many relation repeats the parent's columns on every child row, and a second batched query (WHERE user_id = ANY($1)) is often the cleaner fix. Row counts settle nothing either way, since an inner join drops unmatched rows and a one-to-many join multiplies them, and SQL never requires a join at all.
